claims.text: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility.
Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr has a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
Untreated equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr has inadequate oxygen resistance characterized by rapid oxidation.
Pack aluminization will improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr.
Exposure to an Al-rich powder mixture at elevated temperature induces diffusion of Al into the alloy surface.
Pack aluminization of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will produce a continuous, adherent Al2O3 surface scale.
During high-temperature exposure, diffused Al will react preferentially with oxygen to form Al2O3.
The Al2O3 scale will act as a stable diffusion barrier against further oxygen ingress into the bulk alloy.
Limiting oxygen ingress will minimize oxidation-induced degradation of the alloy.
The aluminization treatment will have limited penetration into the substrate.
Limited treatment penetration will leave the bulk room-temperature ductility and high-temperature strength largely unaffected.
Pack-aluminized specimens will have significantly lower oxidation mass gain than untreated specimens during air exposure at about 800 °C for up to 5 hours.
Pack-aluminized specimens will exhibit slower oxide-scale growth than untreated specimens.
The room-temperature ductility of treated material will remain comparable to that of untreated material.
The 1000 °C yield strength of treated material will remain comparable to that of untreated material.
The predicted oxidation benefit is bounded to static-air exposure near 800 °C for no more than 5 hours.
The treatment must not cause substrate phase changes that compromise mechanical performance at room temperature or 1000 °C.
Mass gain per unit area can be used as a proxy for oxidation extent in the controlled exposure experiment.
The general protective effect of an Al2O3 scale is well established.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts both reduced mass gain and formation of a continuous Al2O3 scale, but the falsification rule grammatically uses a conjunction: failure requires specimens to lack a significant mass-gain reduction while also forming the scale. Consequently, failure to form the predicted scale alone would not clearly falsify the hypothesis.
